title: Locomotor Activity Monitoring in Mice to Study Circadian Rhythms
author: Andrea Brenna
license_note: PMC full-text XML — Bio-protocol — CC-BY confirmed in article XML
materials: Materials and reagents Biological materials 1. 3–6-month-old 129/C57BL6 mice

steps.title: Prepare wheel‑running cages
steps.instruction: Place plastic cages equipped with steel running wheels, add bedding and nesting material, and ensure each cabinet holds no more than 12 cages.

steps.title: Weigh and health‑check mice
steps.instruction: Weigh each 3–6‑month‑old (or 3–5‑month‑old) 129/C57BL6 mouse, assess health, and record data on the veterinary‑approved scoresheet.

steps.title: House mice individually
steps.instruction: Put each mouse alone in a prepared wheel‑running cage with ad libitum food and water.

steps.title: Connect and test magnetic sensor
steps.instruction: Verify that the wheel contains a small magnet in a plastic disc, plug the magnetic‑switch connector near the disc, and test the signal before starting the experiment.

steps.title: Set light/dark timer
steps.instruction: Mount the external timer, program a 12 h light / 12 h dark (LD) cycle, lock the sound‑proof, ventilated cabinets, and turn on two ceiling bulbs (1 000 lux).

substeps.instruction: Confirm light intensity with a luxmeter.

steps.title: Record experimental metadata
steps.instruction: Before starting, note the lighting condition (L:D or D:D), number of recording days, mouse genotype, age, and sex on the designated sheet.

steps.title: Monitor early activity
steps.instruction: Observe mouse wheel‑running activity closely during the first days of the experiment.

steps.title: Entrain mice to LD cycle
steps.instruction: Maintain mice under the 12 h : 12 h LD schedule for at least 10 days so that activity is confined to the night (alpha) phase.

steps.title: Switch to constant darkness
steps.instruction: After ≥10 days, turn off the illumination (after ZT12 for general free‑running measurement; after ZT10 to validate Aschoff‑type II) and keep mice in constant darkness.

steps.title: Record free‑running period
steps.instruction: Allow the free‑running rhythm to continue for at least 10 days, then determine the internal period length (τ) and total revolutions per day.

steps.title: Re‑entrain to LD cycle
steps.instruction: Return mice to the 12 h : 12 h LD schedule for at least 10 days before any phase‑shift experiments.

steps.title: Aschoff‑type II: Light pulse at ZT14
steps.instruction: Apply a 15‑minute light pulse at ZT14 (2 h after lights‑off), then keep mice in constant darkness for 10 days.

steps.title: Aschoff‑type II: Re‑entrain
steps.instruction: Re‑entrain mice to the LD cycle for at least 10 days before the next pulse.

steps.title: Aschoff‑type II: Light pulse at ZT22
steps.instruction: Apply a 15‑minute light pulse at ZT22 (2 h before lights‑on), then keep mice in constant darkness for 10 days.

steps.title: Aschoff‑type II: Re‑entrain again
steps.instruction: Re‑entrain mice to the LD cycle for at least 10 days before the control pulse.

steps.title: Aschoff‑type II: Control pulse at ZT10
steps.instruction: Apply a 15‑minute light pulse at ZT10 (no expected phase shift) and keep mice in constant darkness for 10 days.

steps.title: Calculate circadian time (CT)
steps.instruction: Using each mouse’s free‑running period obtained above, compute the corresponding circadian times (CT) for subsequent light pulses.

steps.title: Aschoff‑type I: Light pulse at CT14
steps.instruction: Apply a 15‑minute light pulse at CT14 (phase delay) while mice remain in constant darkness, then continue recording for 10 days.

steps.title: Aschoff‑type I: Wash‑out period
steps.instruction: Maintain constant darkness for an additional 10 days to eliminate the effect of the previous pulse.

steps.title: Aschoff‑type I: Light pulse at CT22
steps.instruction: Apply a 15‑minute light pulse at CT22 (phase advance) and record for 10 days in constant darkness.

steps.title: Aschoff‑type I: Second wash‑out
steps.instruction: Keep mice in constant darkness for another 10 days before the next pulse.

steps.title: Aschoff‑type I: Light pulse at CT10
steps.instruction: Apply a 15‑minute light pulse at CT10 (no phase shift) and record for 10 days in constant darkness.

steps.title: Optional: Return to LD cycle
steps.instruction: If further experiments are needed, re‑enter mice into the 12 h : 12 h LD schedule.

description: Validation of protocol This protocol or parts of it have been used and validated in the following research articles (among others): • Brenna et al. [24]. Cyclin-dependent kinase 5 (CDK5) regulates the circadian clock. eLife . ( Figure 2 ) • Brenna et al. [16]. Cyclin-dependent kinase 5 (Cdk5) activity is modulated by light and gates rapid phase shifts of the circadian clock. eLife. ( Figure 1 ) • Chavan et al. [25]. Liver-derived ketone bodies are necessary for food anticipation. Nat Commun . (Suppl. Figure 2 ) • Schmutz et al. [26]. A specific role for the REV-ERBα-controlled L-Type Voltage-Gated Calcium Channel CaV1.2 in resetting the circadian clock late at night. J Biol Rhythms . ( Figures 1 and 2 ) Advantages and disadvantages To date, the wheel-running activity is still the best method for extrapolating important information about diurnal/circadian behaviors such as free-running period, phase angle of entrainment to the LD cycle, period amplitude, and daytime running activity. Although numerous methods exist to measure the phase shift of the circadian clock (i.e., monitoring general activity using photo beams or the core body temperature by implanting sensors [27]), the wheel-running activity is still the less invasive approach. Compared to the general activity measurement via photo beams or core temperature, wheel-running measures only voluntary activity and not other activities such as grooming. Due to this, the wheel-running shows clearer onsets and offsets of activity, making the interpretation of an actogram easier. However, there are several points to take into consideration. The lighting conditions should be adjusted via a timer without opening the box. The isolation cabinets are well-ventilated to avoid overheating. However, light is a stronger and more immediate Zeitgeber than temperature. Therefore, the observed temperature variations under LD conditions can be neglected.
